stories.title: Samantha Atlas of Ash Staging: 5 Questions
stories.excerpt: Staging can play a critical role in residential real estate. It helps to bring a model unit to life, and it provides potential renters and buyers with a glimpse of what their future home could look like. Successfully staging requires more than a properly positioned couch and some art on the walls. Enter Ash Staging, a luxury staging and model residence design business that has completed thousands of projects — including commercial and hospitality spaces — over the last 15 years, representing over $50 billion in real estate. Samantha Atlas, senior director of projects at Ash Staging, has been with the firm for nine years. She splits her time between Los Angeles and New York City, and helped to launch the company’s West Coast office. Commercial Observer caught up with Atlas in mid-August to discuss her time with Ash Staging and the value of her work in real estate. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. Commercial Observer: What is the mission of Ash Staging? Samantha Atlas: I’ve been with Ash for a little over nine years now, and really seen it grow. I run the L.A. office, and I joined the company at a time of growth. Since I joined, the story has been, “How do we continue to grow and change the narrative of what staging can be?” Generally speaking, for a long time the idea around staging has been neutrality — nothing with a serious point of view. I came to work at Ash because we sort of eschewed that. We want to imbue personality. We want our clients and our potential buyers of these homes to have an emotional response — it’s what drives us. We believe in the power of paint and will really push our clients to invest outside of the staging into the property to get it sold. What we really believe in, and how we position ourselves as a brand, is being a partner alongside our real estate agents, clients and developers. What are some of the projects that Ash has staged? We just finished staging the 100 Barclay penthouses. These are two gorgeous pent
bullets: Ash Staging completed thousands of projects worth $50B+ across residential, commercial, hospitality over 15 years.
Senior director Samantha Atlas leads Los Angeles office, splits time between LA and NYC markets.
Model unit staging influences renter/buyer perception and decision-making at lease-up and sales phases.
stories.summary: Ash Staging, a luxury staging and model residence design firm, has completed thousands of projects representing over $50 billion in real estate value across residential, commercial, and hospitality sectors over 15 years. Samantha Atlas, senior director of projects, has been with the company for nine years and leads its Los Angeles office. The article focuses on the role of professional staging in helping prospective renters and buyers visualize future homes and make leasing/purchase decisions.
stories.impact: Limited direct relevance to multifamily development strategy. Professional staging is a lease-up and marketing tool that enhances absorption velocity and pricing, but does not affect supply, capital availability, construction costs, or demand fundamentals. Worth considering as a soft cost in pro formas and pre-opening strategy, but not a primary driver of development feasibility or market conditions.

stories.title: Proptech Seed Rounds This Year Are in Full Bloom
stories.excerpt: To the surprise of some, or perhaps many, proptech has reportedly drawn the largest number of $5 million to $10 million seed rounds across industries in 2026. To the surprise of no one, artificial intelligence has a lot to do with those seed rounds. According to a Crunchbase report published July 31, at the top of the scale with $10 million seed rounds are proptech companies such as Breezy, a Los Angeles-based startup offering an AI operating system for residential real estate professionals; Grotto AI, a Manhattan-based IT and Internet firm offering AI-based tools for leasing and renewals; and Hint, a Charlotte, N.C.-based AI‑powered home‑management platform for homeowners. There have been at least 15 proptech seed rounds in the $5 million to $10 million scale so far in 2026, according to Crunchbase, which did not provide an overall number of deals in the category. A Center for Real Estate Technology and Innovation (CRETI) report found 30 deals in the $5 million to $10 million range in the first half of 2026 totaling $207.3 million and representing 4.6 percent of funding across all rounds. Overall proptech venture funding reached $4.53 billion across 231 disclosed funding rounds in the first half of 2026, with a median funding round of $6.75 million. Compared with the prior year, the market was broadly stable. First-half 2026 funding was down 0.6 percent from the first half of 2025 and up 2.6 percent from the first half of 2024, CRETI reported. The total number of seed fundings industry-by-industry is an elusive number. However, according to Seedtable, a global intelligence platform for startups, a typical seed round across industries is $2 million (median), stepping up to $9 million at Series A and $20 million at Series B. Seed is the most common stage by deal count, accounting for 29,708 tracked rounds in 2026. bullets: Proptech seed rounds reach $5M–$10M range, with 15+ deals in H1 2026 totaling $207.3M.
AI-driven platforms: Breezy (LA), Grotto AI (Manhattan), Hint (Charlotte) each raised $10M seeds.
Proptech represents 4.6% of all venture funding; AI tools target leasing, renewals, and property management.
stories.summary: Proptech companies have drawn the largest number of $5 million to $10 million seed rounds across industries in 2026, with at least 15 deals in that range totaling $207.3 million. AI-powered platforms dominate, including Breezy (Los Angeles), Grotto AI (Manhattan), and Hint (Charlotte), each raising $10 million seeds. These tools focus on leasing, renewals, and resident management, with proptech representing 4.6 percent of overall venture funding in the first half of 2026.
stories.impact: AI-driven leasing and property management tools may reduce operational costs and accelerate unit turnover, improving NOI and cap rates. However, widespread adoption could compress leasing spreads and reduce pricing power if competitors gain equal access. Watch for tools that improve tenant retention (reducing vacancy) and streamline renewal cycles—these directly affect asset value in multifamily underwriting. Monitor adoption rates by third-party managers to assess competitive pressure on your asset management advantage.

stories.title: How Landlords Are Cutting Their Eviction Costs
stories.excerpt: By Tom DeRose, co-founder and CEO at PandaGuarantee ___________________________________________________________________________________________ Contested evictions in New York City are the most expensive in the world, running $15,000 to $50,000 each. But the single largest piece of that cost is missed rent, and missed rent is preventable. I started PandaGuarantee because the existing guarantor services were either too slow, too expensive or too confusing to applicants. The customer experience, both of the property owner and their tenants, seemed to be an afterthought. The thesis is simple: The rent guarantee process needs to be as efficient and affordable as possible. Applicant approvals in minutes, economical prices, and an easy to use platform that ties it all together. The $21,000 Problem When landlords think about evictions, they think about lawyers’ fees and court filings. That’s real money, but not where most of the damage is. The majority of the cost is rent — the opportunity cost of having an empty apartment or a squatter not paying for months. In a New York nonpayment proceeding, a landlord can easily go six months (or longer) without collecting while the case sits on the court’s docket. At $3,500 a month — roughly the median for a Manhattan one-bedroom — that’s $21,000 in lost income before you’ve paid a single attorney. Cover the missed rent, and you’ve cut the financial damage roughly in half. That’s the math behind rent guarantee insurance, and it’s why I started PandaGuarantee as a fast, easy, economical option for property owners to protect themselves from tenant default. 2019 Changed the Math Before the Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act (HSTPA), landlords could ask borderline approvable applicants for larger security deposits. That’s no longer an option. The 2019 HSTPA legislation capped security deposits at one month’s rent, and although the legislation was meant to protect renters, the secur
bullets: NYC evictions cost $15K–$50K; missed rent is largest expense, not legal/court fees.
PandaGuarantee offers rent guarantee service with minute-level approvals to reduce landlord vacancy losses.
Nonpayment proceedings in NY can last 6+ months without rent collection, creating major cash-flow drag.
stories.summary: Contested evictions in New York City cost $15,000 to $50,000 each, with missed rent—not legal fees—accounting for the majority of losses. Eviction timelines can stretch six months or longer, leaving landlords without income while cases proceed. PandaGuarantee offers a faster, cheaper rent guarantee and applicant approval service designed to reduce nonpayment risk and vacancy losses.
stories.impact: NYC multifamily developers and operators face significant cash-flow volatility from protracted eviction timelines. Rent guarantee products like PandaGuarantee reduce collection risk and improve underwriting stability, but adoption signals landlord concern over tenant credit quality and payment reliability in the market. If rent guarantees become standard, assume higher lease-up costs and lower effective rents net of guarantor fees. Flag early if NYC protections tighten further—this could erode property-level cash flows and cap-rate assumptions in New York City.

stories.title: Tavaco Properties Buys DMV Office for $29M
stories.excerpt: Tavaco Properties has added another discounted office property to its growing Greater Washington portfolio. The Los Angeles-based firm paid $28.5 million for a 272,300-square-foot building in Falls Church, Va., Business Journals first reported. Hawaii-based James Campbell Company sold the 14-story property at 3110 Fairview Park Drive after acquiring it for $43.7 million in 2016. Tavaco specializes in acquiring and optimizing underperforming assets, and the deal is its third D.C.-area office acquisition since late last year, totaling nearly $65 million. In March, a Tavaco affiliate paid $8.2 million for the 100,900-square-foot Twinbrook Plaza in Rockville, Md., which is about half the $15.5 million that an MRP Realty affiliate paid in 2016. Tavaco also acquired the eight-story, 275,480-square-foot Ballston Station in Arlington for $28 million in late 2025. The State Teachers Retirement System of Ohio had acquired that property for $58.2 million about 30 years ago. “We view Fairview, Ballston Station and Twinbrook Plaza as long-term additions to Tavaco’s portfolio,” Managing Director Sam Tavakoli told the Business Journals in a statement. He also added that the firm expects continued return-to-office trends to support demand for well-operated buildings. Indeed, U.S. office visits rose 6 percent in the first half of the year, although on-site attendance remained 31 percent below 2019 levels. James Campbell Company, meanwhile, has been reducing its national office exposure and concentrating more heavily on industrial assets. Gregory Cornfield can be reached at gcornfield@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Tavaco paid $28.5M for 272K SF office building in Falls Church; seller took 35% loss since 2016.
Tavaco completed 3 DMV-area office acquisitions since late 2024 for ~$65M total; specializes in distressed assets.
Prior sales in region: Twinbrook Plaza 50% below 2016 value; Ballston Station 52% below 30-year-ago price.
stories.summary: Tavaco Properties acquired a 272,300-square-foot office building in Falls Church, Virginia, for $28.5 million, representing a 35 percent loss for the seller (James Campbell Company) since its 2016 purchase at $43.7 million. This is Tavaco's third Greater Washington-area office acquisition since late 2024, totaling approximately $65 million. Prior purchases (Twinbrook Plaza and Ballston Station) also show significant depreciation, indicating severe office market distress in the DMV.
stories.impact: Sustained office distress in Greater Washington reflects structural demand collapse and limited conversion-to-multifamily economics for older office stock. The 35–52 percent haircuts across recent sales suggest cap rates have repriced materially higher, but also signal that ground-up multifamily development may face competition from adaptive-reuse projects at distressed prices. For greenfield multifamily developers, monitor office conversion velocity and pricing in Ballston, Arlington, and Rockville—if landlords can't fill office, they will pivot to residential, potentially depressing new-project land values and rents in those submarkets.

stories.title: Taconic, NREA Add Premium Indian Restaurant to Hell’s Kitchen Mixed-Use
stories.excerpt: Taconic Partners and National Real Estate Advisors have signed a lease with Samudhra at The Ellery, a luxury mixed-use residential development at 312 W. 43rd St. in Hell’s Kitchen. The addition of the New Jersey-based premium Indian restaurant and lounge brings a new full-service dining destination to The Ellery. Samudhra will occupy approximately 10,000 square feet along West 43rd Street. The space will include a dedicated dining area, bar and lounge. The new location will mark Samudhra’s first outpost in New York City and second location overall. “Samudhra brings a premium new dining and social experience that will serve both our residents and the broader neighborhood,” George Tsapelas, SVP with Taconic Partners “From the outset, our vision for The Ellery has been to create a dynamic mixed-use destination that contributes to the energy of the area, and Samudhra further strengthens the retail and dining mix we’ve curated at the property.” Taconic and NREA were represented by Lon Rubackin, Michael Kadosh and Bevan Cohen from CBRE. Samudhra was represented by Brad Schwarz from Lee & Associates. The post Taconic, NREA Add Premium Indian Restaurant to Hell’s Kitchen Mixed-Use appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Taconic/NREA signed Samudhra (premium Indian restaurant/lounge) at The Ellery mixed-use in Hell's Kitchen.
Samudhra occupies 10K SF along West 43rd Street; marks NYC debut and second location overall.
Full-service dining and bar amenities support mixed-use strategy for Hell's Kitchen residential tower.
stories.summary: Taconic Partners and National Real Estate Advisors signed a lease with Samudhra, a premium Indian restaurant and lounge, at The Ellery, a mixed-use residential development at 312 W. 43rd Street in Hell's Kitchen. Samudhra will occupy approximately 10,000 square feet with dedicated dining, bar, and lounge areas, marking its first New York City location and second overall.
stories.impact: Premium restaurant tenancy at street level strengthens The Ellery's mixed-use proposition and resident/neighborhood amenity profile, likely supporting higher residential rents and occupancy. However, this is a single-tenant activation and does not signal broader Hell's Kitchen retail health. Verify ground-floor absorption trends across the submarket; if Samudhra is one of few quality tenants leasing, ground-floor economics may remain challenged for new residential projects, compressing mixed-use development IRRs and extending stabilization timelines.

stories.title: For Southern California, Defense Tech Is the Best Real Estate Offense
stories.excerpt: It’s easy to assume Los Angeles’ biggest contribution to the defense industry and any war effort has been the production of movies and films that celebrate the heroism of combat. But, due to persistent geopolitical instability, combat that’s draining crucial weapon stockpiles, and ongoing efforts to adapt the United States military to the modern demands of high-tech warfare, defense spending is skyrocketing. And no place is benefiting from that more than Southern California, especially the South Bay, a grouping of small cities adjacent to Los Angeles, including Torrance, Hawthorne, Long Beach and El Segundo, that have seen their port-adjacent warehouse spaces transformed into hubs of military manufacturing activity. “The growth curve we’re seeing for the South Bay right now is unprecedented,” said Mac Burridge, a managing director at JLL who leads the advanced manufacturing team. “It’s very akin to the Inland Empire during COVID, where there was just a frenzy for space and only a finite amount available.” Historically, the South Bay has been a hotbed of aeronautics and space technology. Many of the largest traditional defense contractors, known as the primes, operate out of Greater L.A., and SpaceX, which held its blockbuster initial public offering earlier this year, was incubated in the small city of El Segundo, a nexus of startups and innovation just south of Los Angeles International Airport. That tech activity has recently gone into overdrive, a mobilization that has become one of the bright spots of the Southern California economy. A record $366 billion was invested last year in California startups, driven by the AI boom. But the defense tech boom might be even more pronounced. Last summer’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act appropriated $153 billion in defense spending on top of record Pentagon budgets, with a proposed $1.5 trillion of spending for next year. bullets: Defense spending surge benefiting Southern California, especially South Bay (Torrance, Hawthorne, Long Beach, El Segundo).
Port-adjacent warehouse spaces converting to military manufacturing hubs amid geopolitical instability and weapon stockpile depletion.
JLL notes South Bay growth 'unprecedented,' comparable to Inland Empire COVID frenzy; finite space available.
stories.summary: Defense spending is skyrocketing due to geopolitical instability, combat draining weapon stockpiles, and modernization efforts. Southern California's South Bay—including Torrance, Hawthorne, Long Beach, and El Segundo—is experiencing unprecedented growth as port-adjacent warehouse spaces transform into military manufacturing hubs. JLL's advanced manufacturing team notes the growth curve rivals the Inland Empire's COVID-era demand frenzy, with limited space available.
stories.impact: Defense manufacturing expansion in South Bay drives inbound employment and population growth, strengthening rental demand for workforce housing in Long Beach, Torrance, Hawthorne, and El Segundo submarkets. Developers should target Class-B/C multifamily infill near manufacturing clusters and transit. However, industrial land and warehouse space constraints may push developers to adaptive reuse or higher-density residential near ports. Monitor defense contractor hiring announcements (e.g., General Dynamics, Northrop Grumman, Raytheon expansions) to time land acquisition and underwriting windows before rents capitalize gains. Incumbent supply in South Bay is likely tight; new-build projects may command premium rents if delivered before supply influx.

Note grocery retail as a stable, high-occupancy ground-floor tenant in mixed-use residential buildings, but this deal alone does not shift neighborhood rental demand or development strategy.

stories.title: Landmark Properties Delivers 1,261-Bed Student Housing Near USC Campus
stories.excerpt: Landmark Properties has delivered The Standard at Los Angeles, a 429-unit, 1,261-bed student housing community at 3900 South Figueroa St., 0.3 miles from the University of Southern California in Los Angeles. It represents Landmark’s second ground-up development in LA. Rising eight stories, the project was designed by HED, with Landmark Construction, the in-house construction arm of Landmark Properties, serving as general contractor. “We’re excited to open doors at The Standard at Los Angeles and welcome our first residents to our community – just steps from USC’s campus, BMO Stadium and Memorial Coliseum,” said Jason Doornbos, chief development officer at Landmark Properties. “The Standard’s market-leading amenities, design, and luxury unit finishes set a new benchmark for student housing near USC, and this delivery reflects the caliber our team consistently delivers at Landmark.” In 2025, Landmark delivered its first development in the area, The Mark Los Angeles near UCLA, and also acquired Icon Plaza and West 27th Place, which serve students attending USC. bullets: Landmark Properties delivered The Standard at Los Angeles: 429 units, 1,261 beds, 0.3 miles from USC campus.

stories.summary: Landmark Properties delivered The Standard at Los Angeles, a 429-unit, 1,261-bed student housing community located 0.3 miles from the University of Southern California. The eight-story project was designed by HED with Landmark's in-house construction arm as general contractor. This represents Landmark's second ground-up development in Los Angeles, following The Mark near UCLA in 2025 and additional acquisitions serving USC students.
stories.impact: Landmark's rapid USC-area deployment (two ground-ups plus acquisitions in 12 months) signals strong student housing demand and absorption near top-tier universities. For multifamily developers in college towns, track Landmark's stabilization timelines and unit pricing at The Standard to validate student housing economics. However, student housing is a specialized asset class with different demand drivers (enrollment, on-campus housing capacity, institutional policies). General-purpose multifamily developers should monitor if proximity to USC generates spillover demand for workforce/graduate housing and whether supply saturation in student housing depresses nearby conventional rental rates.

stories.title: Inland Completes Equity Raise for St. Paul Opportunity Zone MF Project
stories.excerpt: Inland Real Estate Investment Corporation announced the completion of the approximately $28 million equity raise for Office Conversion Opportunity Zone, LLC, a private real estate investment vehicle structured to qualify as a Qualified Opportunity Fund and sponsored by an affiliate of Inland Investments. The offering has been fully subscribed and is now closed. The fund maintains an approximately 89 percent ownership interest in a 16-story building located at 386 Wabasha Street North in downtown St. Paul, Minnesota. The property is being redeveloped from an underutilized office building into a multifamily residential community featuring 178 apartment units and approximately 2,338 square feet of street-level retail space. The redevelopment is being executed in partnership with Kaeding Development Group LLC as development partner, R.E.C., Inc. d/b/a Ron Clark Construction & Design as general contractor, and Bader Management, Inc. as property manager. If you’re reading about the multifamily industry, you should be in the room with its leaders. Connect Apartments brings together the executives featured in Connect CRE’s coverage for an afternoon of high-level insights and unmatched networking on September 22 at The Biltmore in LA. bullets: Inland completed $28M equity raise for Office Conversion Opportunity Zone project in downtown St. Paul.
16-story building at 386 Wabasha Street North converting to 178 multifamily units + 2,338 SF retail.

stories.summary: Inland Real Estate Investment Corporation closed a $28 million equity raise for a Qualified Opportunity Fund structured to redevelop a 16-story underutilized office building in downtown St. Paul into 178 multifamily units and 2,338 square feet of street-level retail. The property at 386 Wabasha Street North is being developed in partnership with Kaeding Development Group, Ron Clark Construction, and Bader Management.
stories.impact: QOF structure with full equity subscription signals investor appetite for office-to-multifamily conversions in secondary markets (St. Paul) and confidence in tax-deferred capital recycling. Watch for: (1) stabilized rent and occupancy metrics at this asset to validate conversion economics; (2) whether other St. Paul downtown office will follow similar conversion pathways; (3) whether tax incentives are becoming a margin-compressing tool (i.e., developers forced to offer QOF slots to raise equity, signaling weaker fundamentals). If St. Paul multifamily rents soften due to conversion influx, new-build greenfield projects nearby may face headwinds. Track Bader Management's stabilization timeline and unit pricing.

stories.title: Classical Christian School Acquires Permanent Upper West Side Home
stories.excerpt: Denham Wolf Real Estate Services represented The Geneva School of Manhattan in acquiring a permanent Upper West Side campus, securing a long-term home for the independent Classical Christian school. Approved by the United States Bankruptcy Court in July, the acquisition establishes a long-term home for the school. The six-story, 38,838-square-foot educational facility was acquired for $33.2 million and will provide The Geneva School with a permanent campus to support its continued growth and long-term educational mission. The acquisition also represents an exceptional value, with the purchase price significantly below the cost of developing a comparable educational facility in Manhattan today, according to Denham Wolf. Led by Kate Hrobsky and Christopher D. Turner, Denham Wolf served as strategic real estate advisor throughout the acquisition process, providing search strategy, property identification, financial analysis, due diligence, negotiations, and bankruptcy sale advisory. Denham Wolf worked closely with BKREA’s Tom Brady, Ana Barrie, Ryan Candel, and Bob Knakal, who represented the bankruptcy trustees. The post Classical Christian School Acquires Permanent Upper West Side Home appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Geneva School of Manhattan acquired 38,838 SF, six-story Upper West Side campus for $33.2M.
Purchase approved by U.S. Bankruptcy Court; represents 'exceptional value' below new-build cost.
Denham Wolf provided search, financial analysis, due diligence, and bankruptcy advisory; Hrobsky and Turner led team.
stories.summary: The Geneva School of Manhattan, an independent classical Christian school, acquired a permanent Upper West Side campus at 38,838 square feet across six stories for $33.2 million. The acquisition, approved by U.S. Bankruptcy Court in July, provides a long-term educational home at a price significantly below the cost of comparable new construction in Manhattan.
stories.impact: Minimal relevance to multifamily development. Educational facility acquisition from bankruptcy is a distressed-asset transaction and does not reflect residential real estate demand, supply, or capital conditions. However, note that bankruptcy-exit deals signal liquidity stress in Manhattan commercial real estate; if institutional owners are exiting educational properties at steep discounts, broader NYC office/mixed-use markets may face similar pressure. Monitor whether school acquisition signals demand shift away from office/toward alternative uses, which could accelerate office-to-residential conversion activity and compete with greenfield multifamily development on pricing and capital availability.
